deep.reconstruction:
Context: the previous page lists the auxiliary plane triangles attached to a spherical triangle with angles A, B, C and sides a, b, c on the unit sphere. For example, one triangle has angles A, 90°-(A-B+C)/2, 90°-(A+B-C)/2 and opposite sides sin(a/2), sin(b/2)cos(c/2), sin(c/2)cos(b/2). The angle sum works, since A + 180° - A = 180°. These triangles are equivalent to the Gauss (Delambre–Mollweide) analogies. This page restates the content of those triangles as chains of equalities.

(1) 'Man kann dieses auch durch folgende sechs Gleichungen ausdrücken.' Put S = (A+B+C)/2. Then
sinA/sin a = sinB/sin b = sinC/sin c
= -cos S /(2 sin(a/2) sin(b/2) sin(c/2))
= cos((-A+B+C)/2)/(2 sin(a/2) cos(b/2) cos(c/2))
= cos((A-B+C)/2)/(2 cos(a/2) sin(b/2) cos(c/2))
= cos((A+B-C)/2)/(2 cos(a/2) cos(b/2) sin(c/2)).
[Derivation, mine:] apply the plane law of sines in the auxiliary triangles. For instance, the triangle above gives sinA/sin(a/2) = cos((A-B+C)/2)/(sin(b/2)cos(c/2)). Divide both sides by 2cos(a/2) and use sin a = 2 sin(a/2)cos(a/2); this yields the third expression. The triangle with angles 180°-A, S-90°, 90°+(A-B-C)/2 and sides cos(a/2), sin(b/2)sin(c/2), cos(b/2)cos(c/2) gives the -cos S expression in the same way. Together with the spherical sine rule this makes six independent equalities.

(2) Multiply (1) by sin a sin b sin c = 8 Π sin(x/2)cos(x/2). This gives
sinA sin b sin c = sinB sin a sin c = sinC sin a sin b
= -4 cos S cos(a/2)cos(b/2)cos(c/2)
= 4 cos((-A+B+C)/2) cos(a/2) sin(b/2) sin(c/2)
= 4 cos((A-B+C)/2) sin(a/2) cos(b/2) sin(c/2)
= 4 cos((A+B-C)/2) sin(a/2) sin(b/2) cos(c/2).

(3) Gauss identifies this common quantity as 6 times the volume of the tetrahedron O,A,B,C (O the centre, radius 1). In modern terms it is the triple product det(OA,OB,OC) = sin b sin c sinA, von Staudt's 'sine' (polar sine) of the trihedral angle.

(4) The figure is a red-ink sketch. It shows the triangle ABC with an interior point, the circumcentre P, joined to the vertices. This produces three isosceles triangles with paired angles α,α, β,β, γ,γ at the centre. The base angles are labelled (A+B-C)/2 and (A-B+C)/2 at A, and (-A+B+C)/2 at B. The half-sides a/2, b/2, c/2 are cut off by the perpendiculars from P. Solving x+z=A, x+y=B, y+z=C gives base angles x=(A+B-C)/2 etc.
In the right triangle with hypotenuse r and leg c/2 we have tan(c/2) = tan r · cos((A+B-C)/2). Substituting into the last line of (2) gives
6V = 4 cot r sin(a/2) sin(b/2) sin(c/2),
where r is the spherical circumradius.

The next page gives a second, geometric proof. The chord triangle has sides 2 sin(a/2) etc. and planar circumradius sin r. Its area is therefore 2Π sin(x/2)/sin r, and the height of O above its plane is cos r. Hence 6V = 2·area·cos r = 4 cot r Π sin(x/2).
errors: No mathematical errors found. All four expressions in (1) and (2), and the circumradius formula, check out.
Spot checks: trirectangular triangle (all values 1); flat limit, where -cos S ≈ E/2 and E ≈ abc/(4R) recovers sinA/a = 1/(2R).
The volume claim is stated without proof on this page; it is the standard triple-product fact.
The figure tacitly assumes the circumcentre lies inside the triangle, as with any such sketch. The formulas hold generally with signed angles.

results.what: sinA/sin a = -cos((A+B+C)/2)/(2 sin(a/2)sin(b/2)sin(c/2)) and the three companion expressions with one angle sign-flipped, obtained from the plane auxiliary triangles
results.modern_name: Consequences of the Gauss/Delambre(-Mollweide) analogies; expressions for the spherical sine-rule ratio in terms of angle sums and half-sides
results.usually_credited_to: Delambre (1807), Mollweide (1808), Gauss (Theoria motus 1809) for the analogies; such corollaries appear in 19th-century texts

results.what: sinA sin b sin c = -4 cos S cos(a/2)cos(b/2)cos(c/2) = 4cos((-A+B+C)/2)cos(a/2)sin(b/2)sin(c/2) = …
results.modern_name: Expressions for the spherical 'norm'/polar sine (von Staudt's sine of the triangle)
results.usually_credited_to: The quantity itself: Lagrange/Euler (tetrahedron volume), von Staudt 1842 (named 'sine'); these mixed forms are textbook-derivable

results.what: sinA sin b sin c = 6·Vol(OABC) on the unit sphere
results.modern_name: Triple product / volume of the tetrahedron spanned by the centre and the vertices

results.what: 6V = 4 cot r sin(a/2)sin(b/2)sin(c/2), with r the spherical circumradius; equivalently cot r = -cos S cot(a/2)cot(b/2)cot(c/2)
results.modern_name: Formula for the circumradius of a spherical triangle (tan R = tan(a/2)/cos(S-A) family)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th/19th-century spherical trigonometry (Lexell, Euler; textbooks such as Todhunter)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a neat, systematic restatement of the Gauss analogies in sine-rule form, with a tetrahedral-volume interpretation and a circumradius formula. Gauss's authorship of the analogies is well known, and the other results are classical spherical trigonometry. The only modestly notable points are the clean presentation and the early interpretation of the 'sine' of the triangle as six times the tetrahedron volume, before von Staudt (1842).
